etymology: From the third word of the Decalogue, Exodus 20:7; commandment from Latin mandare, to commit or charge.
biblical_def: The Third Commandment is the word of the Decalogue that guards the name of God: "Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain" (Exod 20:7). To take God's name in vain is to use it emptily, lightly, falsely, or irreverently — in cursing and profane swearing, in false oaths and broken vows sworn in His name, in hypocrisy that wears His name without His fear, and in every careless handling of what is holy. The commandment reaches further than the tongue: it requires that the whole of God's self-revelation — His names, titles, attributes, ordinances, word, and works — be used in a holy and reverent way. Positively, it commands the hallowing of God's name, the very first petition the Lord taught us to pray: "Hallowed be thy name" (Matt 6:9). The fearful sanction attached — that the LORD will not hold the violator guiltless — warns that this is no small sin, however small the age accounts it. This dictionary confesses the Third Commandment as binding moral law, abiding under the gospel, for the name of God is great and holy and reverend (Psa 111:9), and those who name the name of Christ must depart from iniquity.
webster_summary: The word of the Decalogue guarding God's name (Exod 20:7): "Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain." It forbids every empty, false, or irreverent use of His name, titles, word, and works, and commands the hallowing of His name — with the warning that He will not hold the violator guiltless.

"Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain."
Forbids profane swearing, false oaths, broken vows, hypocrisy, and all irreverent handling of holy things.
Requires the holy and reverent use of God's names, titles, word, and works.
Carries the sanction: "the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain."
scriptures: Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain.
After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name.
he hath commanded his covenant for ever: holy and reverend is his name.
And ye shall not swear by my name falsely, neither shalt thou profane the name of thy God: I am the LORD.
corruption_summary: The age has emptied the Third Commandment of all force, treating God's name as a common curse-word and reckoning profanity a triviality; the religious corruption is subtler — bearing the name of Christ in hypocrisy, swearing rash vows, and handling holy things carelessly while supposing the commandment is kept because no curse is spoken.
corruption_paragraphs: The open corruption is profanity: the name of God and of Christ has become the common oath of a coarse age, flung into ordinary speech as a curse or an exclamation, with no thought of the One named. The world counts this nothing. God counts it so weighty that He attaches to this commandment, almost alone, the warning that He will not hold the violator guiltless (Exod 20:7). His name is holy and reverend (Psa 111:9); to use it emptily is to despise the God it names.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the text, but the subtler corruption is religious. A man may never curse and still break the Third Commandment grievously — bearing the name of Christ in hypocrisy, swearing what he will not perform, naming God in a prayerless, irreverent way. The principle to recover is reverence: that every use of God's name, word, and works be holy, and that the first prayer of the Christian heart be "Hallowed be thy name" (Matt 6:9). To name the name of God is to be bound to fear it.
roots_summary: From the third word of the Decalogue (Exod 20:7) + Latin mandare (to charge); the commandment guarding the holy and reverent use of God's name.

Sanction: the LORD will not hold the violator guiltless

etymology: From the sixth word of the Decalogue, Exodus 20:13; commandment from Latin mandare, to charge.
biblical_def: The Sixth Commandment is the word of the Decalogue that guards human life: "Thou shalt not kill" (Exod 20:13) — more exactly, thou shalt not murder, the unlawful taking of innocent human life. Its ground is the image of God in man: "Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man" (Gen 9:6). Because every human being bears the divine image, his life is sacred, and to murder him is an assault upon his Maker. The commandment does not forbid all taking of life — it does not forbid the magistrate's lawful execution of the murderer (the same God who said "thou shalt not kill" commanded capital justice in Gen 9:6 and Rom 13:4), nor lawful war, nor the killing of beasts for food. It forbids murder and the heart from which murder springs. For our Lord drives the commandment inward: whosoever is angry with his brother without cause, and whosoever hates his brother, is a murderer in the heart (Matt 5:21–22; 1 John 3:15). Positively, it requires all lawful endeavors to preserve life — our own and our neighbor's. This dictionary confesses the Sixth Commandment as binding moral law, the great wall the law of God sets around the sanctity of human life from the womb to the grave.
webster_summary: The word of the Decalogue guarding human life (Exod 20:13): "Thou shalt not kill" — thou shalt not murder. Grounded in the image of God in man (Gen 9:6), it forbids the unlawful taking of innocent life and the hatred from which it springs (Matt 5:21–22), and requires the preserving of life.
webster_full: SIXTH COMMANDMENT, noun. The sixth word of the Decalogue (Exod 20:13), guarding human life.
"Thou shalt not kill" — more exactly, thou shalt not murder, the unlawful taking of innocent life.
Grounded in the image of God in man (Gen 9:6); to murder is to assault the Maker's image.
Does not forbid lawful execution of the murderer, lawful war, or the killing of beasts.
Driven inward by Christ: unjust anger and hatred are murder of the heart (Matt 5:21–22).
scriptures: Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man.
But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment.
Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer: and ye know that no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him.
corruption_summary: The age cheapens the Sixth Commandment from both ends: it shrinks the sanctity of life so that the unborn, the aged, and the inconvenient may be killed under softening names, and it widens "thou shalt not kill" into a pacifism that forbids the magistrate his God-given sword and the murderer his just penalty.
corruption_paragraphs: The gravest corruption of the Sixth Commandment in our day is the assault on innocent life under gentle names — the unborn child destroyed and called a choice, the aged and suffering killed and called mercy. But the commandment guards the image of God in man (Gen 9:6), and that image is borne by the smallest hidden child in the womb. To take that life is murder, however the age relabels it. The dictionary names abortion and euthanasia as violations of this commandment.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the text, but the words are also stretched the wrong way. Some read "thou shalt not kill" to forbid all taking of life — the magistrate's execution of the murderer, the soldier's lawful war. But the same God who forbade murder commanded capital justice (Gen 9:6) and armed the magistrate with the sword (Rom 13:4). The principle to recover is precise: the commandment forbids murder — the unlawful taking of innocent life — and the hatred behind it (1 John 3:15), and requires every lawful means of preserving life, from the womb to the grave.
roots_summary: From the sixth word of the Decalogue (Exod 20:13); the commandment forbidding murder and the hatred behind it, grounded in the image of God in man (Gen 9:6).

usage: The Sixth Commandment guards the sanctity of life from the womb to the grave.

etymology: From the eighth word of the Decalogue, Exodus 20:15; commandment from Latin mandare, to charge.
biblical_def: The Eighth Commandment is the word of the Decalogue that guards property and honest dealing: "Thou shalt not steal" (Exod 20:15). It forbids the taking of what is another's by theft, robbery, fraud, false weights, oppression, the withholding of wages, usury, and every dishonest gain. By guarding the neighbor's goods it upholds the lawful right of property, which Scripture everywhere assumes — for one cannot steal what is held in common, and the command itself supposes that men rightly own what is theirs. Positively, it requires honest labor, fair dealing, the paying of debts and wages, faithful stewardship, and a generous hand to the poor: "Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth" (Eph 4:28). So the commandment turns the thief into a worker and the worker into a giver. It reaches the heart, forbidding covetousness, the root of theft, and the greed that is idolatry (Col 3:5). This dictionary confesses the Eighth Commandment as binding moral law, upholding both the right of property and the duty of charity, and condemning theft whether done by the burglar, the swindler, the oppressor of the poor, or the tax-gatherer who robs by the color of law.
webster_summary: The word of the Decalogue guarding property and honest dealing (Exod 20:15): "Thou shalt not steal." It forbids theft, fraud, false weights, oppression, and dishonest gain; upholds the lawful right of property; and requires honest labor, fair dealing, and a generous hand to the needy (Eph 4:28).
webster_full: EIGHTH COMMANDMENT, noun. The eighth word of the Decalogue (Exod 20:15), guarding property and honest dealing.
"Thou shalt not steal" — forbidding theft, robbery, fraud, false weights, and oppression.
Upholds the lawful right of property, which the command itself assumes.
Requires honest labor, fair dealing, the paying of wages, and faithful stewardship.
Turns the thief into a worker and the worker into a giver (Eph 4:28).
scriptures: Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth.
Thou shalt not defraud thy neighbour, neither rob him: the wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night until the morning.
A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight.
corruption_summary: The Eighth Commandment is corrupted by those who keep its letter while breaking its spirit — the respectable fraud, the unjust weight, the withheld wage — and by ideologies that deny the right of property the commandment upholds, calling the redistribution of another man's goods justice rather than the theft it is.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is the gentleman thief: the man who would never break into a house but defrauds in his business, uses a false balance (Prov 11:1), withholds the laborer's wage (Lev 19:13), or profits by oppressing the poor. The commandment reaches all of these. Theft wears a suit as often as a mask, and the dictionary names the respectable forms — fraud, exploitation, the dishonest gain dressed as good business — as true breaches of the Eighth Commandment.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the text, but a deeper corruption denies the very right of property the commandment assumes. Ideologies that treat private ownership as itself oppression, and the seizing of another man's goods as justice, stand the commandment on its head: "thou shalt not steal" presupposes that a man may rightly own. The principle to recover is the whole counsel: the right of property is real and guarded, and so is the duty of charity — honest labor that one may have to give to him that needeth (Eph 4:28). The commandment condemns both the burglar and the system that robs by law, and commands the open hand.
roots_summary: From the eighth word of the Decalogue (Exod 20:15); the commandment forbidding theft and fraud, upholding the right of property and the duty of honest labor and charity.

etymology: From ceremonial (Latin caerimonia, a sacred rite) + law; the ritual ordinances of Moses — sacrifices, priesthood, feasts, purities — fulfilled in Christ.
biblical_def: The ceremonial law is that part of the law given through Moses which concerned the worship and ritual life of Israel: the sacrifices and offerings, the priesthood and tabernacle, the feasts and sabbaths, the clean and unclean, circumcision and the purities. The Reformed tradition has long distinguished, within the one law of God, three uses or kinds: the moral law (the Ten Commandments, the abiding rule of righteousness), the judicial or civil law (the ordering of Israel as a nation, whose general equity continues), and the ceremonial law (the shadows of things to come). The ceremonial law was never an end in itself; it was a great preaching of the gospel in type and shadow, pointing forward to Christ. Every lamb slain, every priest interceding, every feast kept, was a finger pointing to Him who is the true Lamb, the true Priest, the true Passover. Therefore, when Christ came and fulfilled them, the ceremonies passed away: the veil was torn, the sacrifices ceased, the wall between Jew and Gentile fell. "Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday... which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ" (Col 2:16–17). This dictionary confesses that the ceremonial law was holy and good, fully fulfilled and abrogated in Christ, and now read not for ritual obligation but for the gospel it everywhere preaches.
webster_summary: The ritual part of the Mosaic law — sacrifices, priesthood, feasts, purities — distinguished from the abiding moral law and the judicial law. A great preaching of the gospel in type and shadow, pointing to Christ, and fulfilled and abrogated in Him (Col 2:16–17).
webster_full: CEREMONIAL LAW, noun. The ritual ordinances of the Mosaic law — sacrifices, priesthood, feasts, and purities.
Distinguished in the Reformed tradition from the moral law and the judicial (civil) law.
Never an end in itself, but a preaching of the gospel in type and shadow.
Every sacrifice and feast pointed forward to Christ — the true Lamb, Priest, and Passover.
Fulfilled and abrogated in Christ; the shadow gives way to the body (Col 2:16–17).
scriptures: Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ.

For the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with those sacrifices which they offered year by year continually make the comers thereunto perfect.
Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us.
Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.
corruption_summary: The ceremonial law is corrupted by two opposite errors: a Judaizing that would bind its shadows on the Christian conscience again — sabbaths, feasts, food laws — as though Christ had not fulfilled them, and a careless dispensationalism or antinomianism that, in casting off the ceremonies, throws out the abiding moral law along with them.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is to re-impose the shadows. Whether in the old Judaizers who troubled Galatia, or in modern movements that bind festival-keeping, food laws, or ceremonial sabbaths upon believers, the error is the same: to go back to the shadow when the body has come. Paul forbids it — let no man judge you in meat, drink, or holy day, which are a shadow; the body is of Christ (Col 2:16–17). To cling to the type is to deny that the Lamb has come.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, but the opposite corruption confuses the kinds of law. Some, rightly seeing the ceremonial law abrogated, sweep away the moral law with it, as though the Ten Commandments too were shadows that passed at the cross. They were not. Christ came not to destroy but to fulfil (Matt 5:17); the ceremonial law is fulfilled and gone, but the moral law abides as the rule of the redeemed life. The principle to recover is the careful distinction: the shadows are fulfilled in Christ and read now for the gospel they preach, while the moral law stands.

etymology: From magistrate (Latin magister, a master, ruler) + sword; the coercive authority God grants the civil ruler in Romans 13:4.
biblical_def: The magistrate's sword is the Scripture's name for the coercive authority God has given to the civil ruler — the lawful power to punish evildoers, even unto death. Paul sets it forth in Romans 13: the ruler is the minister of God, "for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil" (Rom 13:4). The sword is no human invention but a divine ordinance: God has appointed the magistrate to bear it for the restraint of wickedness and the protection of the good, so that the world is not given over to violence and anarchy. This is the ground of lawful government, lawful policing, just war, and capital justice. The same God who forbade private murder in the Sixth Commandment armed the public magistrate to execute the murderer (Gen 9:6), and the two stand together without contradiction: vengeance belongs to God, who has delegated a measure of it to the ordained magistrate, while forbidding it to the private hand (Rom 12:19). The magistrate's sword is to be used justly, under God, for the punishment of evil and the praise of good (1 Pet 2:14). This dictionary confesses the civil sword as a God-ordained authority, rejecting both the anarchism that denies it and the tyranny that abuses it.
webster_summary: The Scripture's name for the coercive authority God grants the civil ruler — the lawful power to punish evildoers, even unto death (Rom 13:4). A divine ordinance for the restraint of wickedness and protection of the good, to be used justly under God, rejecting both anarchism and tyranny.

The ground of lawful government, just war, and capital justice (Gen 9:6).

scriptures: for he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man.
Or unto governors, as unto them that are sent by him for the punishment of evildoers, and for the praise of them that do well.
Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.
corruption_summary: The magistrate's sword is corrupted by the anarchist and pacifist who deny the ruler any God-given power of coercion, and by the tyrant who wields it not for the punishment of evil and praise of good but for his own oppression — both forgetting that the sword is God's ordinance, held in trust and accountable to Him.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption denies the sword altogether: the pacifist who reads "resist not evil" (a word to the private man about personal retaliation) as binding the magistrate to bear no sword, and the anarchist who would abolish coercive authority entirely. But Paul calls the sword-bearing ruler the minister of God (Rom 13:4); to deny the sword is to deny the ordinance that restrains a fallen world from devouring itself. The dictionary names the magistrate's coercive authority as God-given and good.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, but the opposite corruption is older and bloodier: the tyrant who bears the sword not as God's minister for good but for his own glory and oppression, punishing the righteous and praising the wicked. The sword is held in trust. The principle to recover is the whole biblical teaching: the magistrate's sword is a divine ordinance (Rom 13:4), to be used justly for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good (1 Pet 2:14), under God and accountable to Him — never to be abolished by the anarchist, never to be absolutized by the tyrant.

etymology: From Greek eidolon (an image) + latreia (worship, service); the worship of any thing or being in the place of the living God.
biblical_def: Idolatry is the worship or supreme love of anything in the place of the living God — the first and most basic of all sins, forbidden in the first two commandments and condemned throughout Scripture. The First Commandment forbids having any other god; the Second forbids worshipping the true God by images. But idolatry is wider than carved figures and pagan altars. It is, at root, a matter of the heart: whatever a man fears, loves, trusts, and serves above God is his idol, whether it be a graven image, a false deity, money (covetousness is idolatry, Col 3:5), the belly, pleasure, power, or the self. Paul exposes the inward engine of all idolatry in Romans 1: men knew God, but glorified Him not as God, and changed the glory of the incorruptible God into images, worshipping and serving the creature more than the Creator (Rom 1:21–25). Every idol is a robbery of the honor due to God alone and a lie about reality, for an idol is nothing in the world (1 Cor 8:4) and they that make them become like them (Psa 115:8). The remedy is not merely to smash the images but to turn from idols to serve the living and true God (1 Thess 1:9). This dictionary confesses idolatry as the great sin against the glory of God, exposed and slain only by the gospel that turns the heart back to its true Lord.
webster_summary: The worship or supreme love of anything in the place of the living God — forbidden in the first two commandments and the root sin of the human heart. Wider than carved images: whatever a man fears, loves, and trusts above God (covetousness is idolatry, Col 3:5). The remedy is to turn from idols to the living God (1 Thess 1:9).

Forbidden in the First Commandment (no other gods) and the Second (no images).
Wider than carved figures: a matter of the heart's supreme fear, love, and trust.
Covetousness is idolatry (Col 3:5); the self, pleasure, and power may be idols.
The remedy: to turn from idols to serve the living and true God (1 Thess 1:9).
scriptures: Thou shalt have no other gods before me.
Who changed the truth of God into a lie, and worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen.
Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth... and covetousness, which is idolatry.
how ye turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God.
corruption_summary: The modern man supposes idolatry an ancient and outgrown sin, since he bows to no carved image, and so misses the idols of his own heart — money, sex, self, the state, the autonomous will — while a sentimental religion redefines even the worship of false gods as a valid path, calling idolatry diversity.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is the comfortable assumption that idolatry is a primitive sin the modern world has left behind. No one in the city bows to a statue, so idolatry is reckoned obsolete. But idolatry was never chiefly about the wood and stone; it is about the heart that loves, fears, and trusts something more than God. The covetous man is an idolater (Col 3:5); so is the man whose god is his belly, his pleasure, his career, his nation, or his own sovereign will. The idols have changed their dress, not their nature.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word, but a sentimental religiosity now recasts the worship of false gods as a legitimate diversity of spiritual paths, so that to name idolatry as sin is thought intolerant. Scripture knows no such tolerance: men have changed the truth of God into a lie and worshipped the creature more than the Creator (Rom 1:25), and there is one living and true God to whom alone worship is due. The principle to recover is both the breadth and the seriousness of idolatry: it is the root sin of every heart, and its only cure is to turn from idols to serve the living God (1 Thess 1:9).

etymology: From weight (Old English gewiht) and measure (Latin mensura); the standards of honest trade, which Scripture makes a matter of righteousness before God.
biblical_def: Weights and measures — the stones and balances and ephahs by which the ancient world bought and sold — are made by Scripture a matter of righteousness, not mere commerce, for the man who falsifies them robs his neighbor and offends his God. The merchant of old carried weights in his bag and measures in his shop; to keep two sets, a heavy stone for buying and a light one for selling, a large measure to receive and a small to give, was a common and hidden fraud. The law forbade it: "Thou shalt not have in thy bag divers weights, a great and a small... But thou shalt have a perfect and just weight, a perfect and just measure shalt thou have" (Deut 25:13–15). And the proverb states the principle as God's own concern: "A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight" (Prov 11:1); "Divers weights, and divers measures, both of them are alike abomination to the LORD" (Prov 20:10). The prophets thundered against the merchants who made the ephah small and the shekel great and falsified the balances by deceit (Amos 8:5). This dictionary confesses that honest weights and measures are a matter of the heart's integrity before God: the God who sees the scales in the dark delights in the just weight and abhors the false, and true religion shows itself in the marketplace as much as in the sanctuary.
webster_summary: The standards of honest trade — balances, weights, and measures — which Scripture makes a matter of righteousness before God. The law forbids the double weight and false balance (Deut 25:13–15); a just weight is the LORD's delight and a false balance His abomination (Prov 11:1; 20:10).
webster_full: WEIGHTS AND MEASURES, noun phrase. The standards of honest trade, made by Scripture a matter of righteousness.

"A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight" (Prov 11:1).
"Divers weights, and divers measures... are alike abomination to the LORD" (Prov 20:10).
The prophets condemned merchants who falsified the balances by deceit (Amos 8:5).
scriptures: A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight.
But thou shalt have a perfect and just weight, a perfect and just measure shalt thou have: that thy days may be lengthened in the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.
Divers weights, and divers measures, both of them are alike abomination to the LORD.
making the ephah small, and the shekel great, and falsifying the balances by deceit.
corruption_summary: The fraud of false weights never died; it only changed its instruments — the hidden fee, the misleading label, the rigged contract, the deceptive measure — and a privatized morality that imagines God indifferent to business dealings forgets that the LORD Himself weighs the scales and abhors the false balance.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is as old as trade and as new as the latest deception: the double weight, the false balance, the small ephah and the great shekel (Amos 8:5). The instruments change — the hidden charge, the doctored measure, the fine print framed to deceive, the contract written to rob — but the sin is one: defrauding the neighbor in the marketplace while keeping a respectable face. Scripture lifts this out of mere commerce and sets it before God: a false balance is His abomination (Prov 11:1).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, but a privatized morality imagines that religion belongs to the heart and the sanctuary while business runs by its own rules. Scripture knows no such division. The God who delights in a just weight (Prov 11:1) sees the scales in the dark shop, and He ties honest measures to His blessing in the land (Deut 25:15). The principle to recover is the integration of faith and trade: true religion is honest in the marketplace, and the just weight is the LORD's delight.
roots_summary: From weight (Old English gewiht) and measure (Latin mensura); the standards of honest trade, which Scripture makes a matter of righteousness before God.
roots_lines: Old English gewiht (weight) and Latin mensura (measure)
The stones, balances, and ephahs of ancient trade
The law forbids divers weights and measures (Deut 25:13–15)
A just weight is the LORD's delight; a false balance His abomination (Prov 11:1)
The prophets condemned the falsified balance (Amos 8:5)
usage: Honest weights and measures are, in Scripture, a matter of righteousness before God.
"A false balance is abomination to the LORD" lifts weights and measures out of mere commerce.
The God who sees the scales in the dark shop delights in just weights and measures.

etymology: From Hebrew Yom Kippur (day of covering / atonement); the great annual day of Leviticus 16 when Israel's sins were covered, fulfilled in Christ.
biblical_def: The Day of Atonement (Hebrew Yom Kippur, "day of covering") was the most solemn day of Israel's year, appointed in Leviticus 16, when atonement was made for all the sins of the people and the sanctuary itself was cleansed. Once a year, and only on this day, the high priest entered the Most Holy Place, behind the veil, into the very presence of God above the mercy seat — and not without blood. Two goats were taken: one was slain as a sin offering, its blood carried within and sprinkled upon the mercy seat; over the other, the live goat, the high priest confessed all the iniquities of Israel, laying them on its head, and it was led away into the wilderness, bearing their sins to a land not inhabited — the scapegoat. So the two goats together preached one atonement: the death that satisfies and the bearing-away that removes. The whole day was a shadow of Christ. The Epistle to the Hebrews draws it out: Christ is the true High Priest who entered once into the holy place, not with the blood of goats and calves but by His own blood, having obtained eternal redemption (Heb 9:11–12). He is the slain goat whose blood satisfies and the scapegoat who bears our sins away. This dictionary confesses the Day of Atonement as a great gospel-shadow, wholly fulfilled in the once-for-all sacrifice of Christ.
webster_summary: Israel's most solemn day (Lev 16, Yom Kippur), when the high priest entered the Most Holy Place with blood and atonement was made for all the people's sins. The two goats — one slain, one bearing sins into the wilderness — preached one atonement, fulfilled in Christ, our true High Priest (Heb 9:11–12).

Once a year the high priest entered the Most Holy Place, behind the veil, not without blood.

The live goat (scapegoat) bore the confessed sins of Israel into the wilderness.
A shadow of Christ, our true High Priest, who entered by His own blood (Heb 9:11–12).
scriptures: For on that day shall the priest make an atonement for you, to cleanse you, that ye may be clean from all your sins before the LORD.
Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us.
And the goat shall bear upon him all their iniquities unto a land not inhabited: and he shall let go the goat in the wilderness.
but now once in the end of the world hath he appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.
corruption_summary: The Day of Atonement is robbed of its meaning when read as a mere primitive ritual of blood, an ancient cleansing now outgrown, rather than as the God-given shadow of the cross; the deeper modern corruption is the recoil from blood atonement itself, which would empty both the type and its fulfillment of their offense and their power.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption reads the Day of Atonement as primitive religion — bloody, archaic, embarrassing — a ritual humanity has thankfully left behind. But the day was no mere ritual; it was a divinely-designed preaching of the gospel. The slain goat and the scapegoat together teach what the cross would accomplish: sin punished and sin removed, the death that satisfies and the bearing-away that carries guilt into a land not inhabited (Lev 16:22). To despise the shadow is to despise the substance.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the text, but the age recoils from the blood the day requires, and that recoil reaches the cross. Theologies that reject substitutionary atonement as "cosmic child abuse" or primitive cruelty are repudiating what the Day of Atonement foreshadowed. The principle to recover is the necessity and the glory of blood atonement: on that day atonement was made to cleanse from all sins (Lev 16:30); and Christ, once in the end of the world, has appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of Himself (Heb 9:26). The Day of Atonement is fulfilled, and its blood was the shadow of the better blood that speaks.
roots_summary: From Hebrew Yom Kippur (day of covering); Israel's annual day of atonement (Lev 16), a shadow of Christ's once-for-all sacrifice.

etymology: From refuge (Latin refugium, a fleeing-back, a shelter); the six Levitical cities of Numbers 35 and Joshua 20, appointed as a shelter for the manslayer.
biblical_def: The cities of refuge were six cities appointed in Israel, three on each side of the Jordan, to which a man who had killed another unintentionally might flee and be safe from the avenger of blood until he could stand trial (Num 35; Josh 20). The law distinguished sharply between the murderer and the manslayer: the murderer, who killed with hatred and lying in wait, was to die, for blood defiles the land and only the blood of the murderer cleanses it (Num 35:33); but the man who killed by accident, without enmity, was not to be given over to the avenger's vengeance. For him God provided a refuge. He fled to the nearest city, was received, and there abode in safety until the death of the high priest, when he might return home free. The cities of refuge thus joined justice and mercy: they upheld the sanctity of life and the just punishment of murder, while sheltering the innocent-in-intent from blood-vengeance. And they preached the gospel in shadow. The man fleeing for his life to a place of refuge, safe only so long as he remained within it, is a picture of the sinner who flees to Christ — the refuge set before us, in whom alone there is safety from the avenging justice of God (Heb 6:18). This dictionary confesses the cities of refuge as a monument of God's justice and mercy and a type of Christ our refuge.
webster_summary: The six Levitical cities (Num 35; Josh 20) to which the unintentional manslayer might flee for safety from the avenger of blood until trial. They joined justice and mercy — upholding the punishment of murder while sheltering the innocent-in-intent — and prefigured Christ, the refuge to whom the sinner flees (Heb 6:18).

Three on each side of the Jordan, to which the unintentional killer might flee.
They distinguished the murderer (who must die) from the manslayer (who is sheltered).
The manslayer abode safe until the death of the high priest, then returned home free.
A type of Christ, the refuge to whom the sinner flees for safety (Heb 6:18).
scriptures: Then ye shall appoint you cities to be cities of refuge for you; that the slayer may flee thither, which killeth any person at unawares.
These were the cities appointed for all the children of Israel, and for the stranger that sojourneth among them, that whosoever killeth any person at unawares might flee thither.
that... we might have a strong consolation, who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us.
So ye shall not pollute the land wherein ye are: for blood it defileth the land.
corruption_summary: The cities of refuge are corrupted when read as mere ancient legal procedure, missing both their careful justice — which the modern world abandons by softening murder — and their gospel shadow, the refuge from divine wrath that points to Christ; a sentimental reading also blurs the law's sharp line between murder and manslaughter.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is to read the cities of refuge as a quaint piece of ancient jurisprudence and nothing more. But the law is precise and weighty: it upholds the sanctity of life, refusing to let bloodshed pollute the land (Num 35:33), and it draws a sharp line between the murderer who must die and the manslayer who is sheltered — a justice the modern world abandons when it softens murder and blurs intent. The cities of refuge teach a God who is at once just and merciful.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the text, but the larger loss is the gospel shadow. The man who has incurred the death-penalty of the avenger flees for his life to the appointed refuge and is safe only within it — a living picture of the sinner who flees to lay hold on the hope set before him (Heb 6:18). The principle to recover is Christ our refuge: as the manslayer ran for the city gate, so the sinner runs to Christ, in whom alone there is shelter from the avenging justice of God, and outside whom there is none.
roots_summary: From Latin refugium (a shelter); the six Levitical cities (Num 35; Josh 20) sheltering the manslayer — God's justice and mercy, and a type of Christ our refuge.

etymology: From Latin restaurare (to renew, rebuild); the biblical theme of God's restoring of His people and His creation — not to be confused with universalist "restoration of all things."
biblical_def: Restoration is the biblical theme of God's renewing, rebuilding, and making whole — of His people, His worship, and at last His whole creation. It runs through Scripture. God restores the penitent backslider: "He restoreth my soul" (Psa 23:3); He promises to restore the years the locust hath eaten (Joel 2:25); He restores Job's estate when Job prays for his friends (Job 42:10). He restores His people from captivity, bringing Judah home from Babylon to rebuild the temple and the walls. He restores the fallen by the gospel, charging the spiritual to restore an overtaken brother in the spirit of meekness (Gal 6:1). And He will restore all things in the consummation — "the times of restitution of all things, which God hath spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets" (Acts 3:21) — when Christ returns, the dead are raised, and the creation itself is delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God (Rom 8:21). This is the new heavens and new earth wherein dwelleth righteousness. But the dictionary marks a sharp boundary: the biblical "restitution of all things" is the renewal of the redeemed creation, not the universalist heresy that all persons, and even the devils, will at last be saved. Restoration is glorious and real; it is not universal salvation. This dictionary confesses the doctrine of restoration as the renewing work of God, climaxing in the new creation, while rejecting the Origenist apokatastasis that empties hell.
webster_summary: The biblical theme of God's renewing and making whole — the penitent soul (Psa 23:3), the captive people, the fallen brother (Gal 6:1), and at last the whole creation (Acts 3:21; Rom 8:21). A real and glorious doctrine, sharply distinguished from the universalist heresy that all persons and even devils will be saved.
webster_full: RESTORATION (DOCTRINE OF), noun. The biblical theme of God's renewing, rebuilding, and making whole.
He restores the soul (Psa 23:3) and the years the locust hath eaten (Joel 2:25).
He restores His people from captivity, and the fallen brother by the gospel (Gal 6:1).
He will restore all things in the consummation — the new heavens and new earth (Acts 3:21).
Sharply distinct from the universalist heresy that all persons and devils will be saved.
scriptures: Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things, which God hath spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets since the world began.
He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake.
Because the creature itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God.
Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness.
corruption_summary: The good word "restoration" is hijacked by the universalist, who reads "the restitution of all things" (Acts 3:21) to mean that every person, and even Satan and his angels, will finally be saved and hell at last emptied — a heresy as old as Origen and condemned by the church, which denies the eternal judgment Scripture plainly teaches.
corruption_paragraphs: The chief corruption of the doctrine of restoration is universalism. Origen taught an apokatastasis, a final restoration in which all rational creatures — even the devil — would be reconciled to God and hell emptied; the church condemned it. The heresy lives in modern dress wherever men press "the restitution of all things" (Acts 3:21) into a promise that none shall finally perish. But the same Scripture that promises the restoration of the creation also teaches an eternal hell, a final judgment, and a fixed gulf. Restoration is the renewing of the redeemed and their world; it is not the salvation of all.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond this old heresy in new sentiment — the "larger hope" that God's love would not allow any to be finally lost. The principle to recover is the careful boundary: the restitution of all things is the consummation of redemption — the soul restored (Psa 23:3), the creation freed from corruption (Rom 8:21), the new heavens and new earth — and it shines all the brighter against the dark fact of an eternal judgment for the unrepentant. Restoration is glorious because it is not universal; it is the inheritance of those who are Christ's.
roots_summary: From Latin restaurare (to renew); God's renewing of soul, people, and creation, climaxing in the new heavens and earth — not the universalist salvation of all.

usage: The doctrine of restoration runs from "He restoreth my soul" to the new heavens and new earth.
